subject: Outbound address governance for private endpoints
messages:
From: Laila Ahmed <networkops@aurorahealth.com>
To: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.example.com>
Cc: Thomas Reed <procurement@aurorahealth.com>
Date: 2028-07-18T08:12:00-07:00
Subject: Outbound address governance for private endpoints

Hi Jonas,

Thanks for taking this on. As we move Redwood into Aurora Health's VPC-attached private deployment, our security and procurement teams need a tight, auditable plan for outbound connectivity. Specifically we need: 

- A definitive list (IP addresses or CIDR blocks) that our perimeter firewall team can allowlist for all Redwood control-plane callbacks and health checks.
- Ports and protocols you expect back to our hosts (e.g., 443, 853 if DNS over TLS, mTLS endpoints).
- Whether you support allowlisting by FQDN/SNI alone and any guidance on TLS validation (we prefer mTLS where possible).
- A short mutual action plan (MAP) with owners and dates so procurement can close the SOC/security checklist.

Attached is our security questionnaire and a sketch of our network zones. Can you confirm and propose next steps?

Laila
Network Operations
Aurora Health

Attachments: aurora_security_questionnaire_v2.pdf
From: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.example.com>
To: Laila Ahmed <networkops@aurorahealth.com>
Cc: Jasmine Liu <jasmine_liu@redwood.example.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.example.com>, Thomas Reed <procurement@aurorahealth.com>
Date: 2028-07-18T10:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Outbound address governance for private endpoints

Hi Laila — thanks for the clear ask. Quick summary up front: we can support both static egress IPs and hostname-based allowlisting depending on your operational constraints; we recommend a layered approach (static egress for control-plane + optional FQDN allowlist for ancillary services). Below is what I propose as an initial plan and what we need from you to finalize.

What Redwood can provide today
- Control plane callback IP set (regional CIDRs) for health checks, audit/webhook callbacks, and telemetry: we will provide short-lived published CIDRs and a weekly digest with change windows.
- Ports: primarily TCP/443. For DNS-over-TLS (optional) we may use 853. If you require mTLS we can enable client cert authentication for callbacks.
- FQDN option: yes — callback endpoints use TLS with strict SNI and we publish our cert pins. However many enterprise customers prefer IP allowlisting for egress enforcement.

Options (trade-offs)
1) Static egress NAT (recommended for strict firewalls): Redwood dedicates NAT block(s) per deployment. Pros: simple firewall rules; minimal ops for you. Cons: IP rotation windows for maintenance; requires acceptance of published CIDRs.
2) Proxying via customer-managed outbound proxy: Your proxy handles egress and Redwood hits your proxy endpoints. Pros: you maintain full control and inspection. Cons: added latency and proxy config.
3) FQDN-only allowlist with mTLS: We recommend this if you prefer cert-based authentication and don't want to maintain IPs. Pros: avoids IP churn. Cons: some firewalls cannot enforce solely on FQDN.

Needed from Aurora to finalize
- Confirm deployment topology (on-prem VM, cloud VPC with TGW/Transit, or hybrid with NAT Gateway).
- Confirm whether your perimeter allows FQDN-based rules or strictly requires IP/CIDR.
- Any required PA/PAK dates for procurement to close.

Next steps / MAP proposal
- Today (Jonas): provide draft CIDRs + port list (by EOD).
- 2028-07-20 (Aurora): confirm topology and policy preference.
- 2028-07-22 (Jasmine & Jonas): sign off on final allowlist and provide signed evidence pack (SOC traces + IP digest).

I attached a short spreadsheet with the architecture options so you can mark preferences. Happy to jump on a quick call if that speeds things up.

Thanks,
Jonas Weber
Sr. Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Attachments: egress_arch_options.xlsx
From: Laila Ahmed <networkops@aurorahealth.com>
To: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.example.com>
Cc: Jasmine Liu <jasmine_liu@redwood.example.com>, Thomas Reed <procurement@aurorahealth.com>
Date: 2028-07-18T12:30:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Outbound address governance for private endpoints

Jonas — appreciate the clear breakdown. Two quick follow ups from our side: 

1) Control plane reachability: Does Redwood require callbacks to the control plane for policy decisions during inference, or are those only for telemetry/health? We need to know if an outage to the control plane would impact inference.

2) IP specificity: your note about "short-lived published CIDRs" — will you provide a stable delegated prefix per-customer or a rotating public pool? We need to determine whether we can accept periodic updates to the allowlist without lengthy change windows.

We've also attached a high-level network topology so you can see how our NAT and inspection sit in the flow. Proposed call: 2028-07-19 09:00 PDT to align owners. Can you confirm?

Laila

Attachments: network_topology.png
From: Jasmine Liu <jasmine_liu@redwood.example.com>
To: Laila Ahmed <networkops@aurorahealth.com>, Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.example.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.example.com>, Thomas Reed <procurement@aurorahealth.com>
Date: 2028-07-18T15:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Outbound address governance for private endpoints

Hi Laila — quick answers and a narrow deliverable set so procurement can close the checklist.

Short answers
- Control plane impact: inference is served from your dedicated nodes; control-plane callbacks are used for non-blocking telemetry, async model updates, and feature flagging. In normal operation an outbound failure to the control plane will not stop in-flight inference RPCs. However, model rollout decisions and new connection handshakes that rely on feature flags may be impacted. If you require zero dependence we can coordinate a fully self-contained private deployment (extra SLA and licensing).
- CIDR model: we can support a customer-dedicated NAT CIDR / small set of static IPs for the duration of your contract (preferred for minimal churn). For customers who cannot accept static blocks we support a published rotating pool but require a 72-hour change window notification.

Published (example) control-plane ranges for your firewall rules (please allowlist these with TCP/443):
- 34.120.64.0/21  (controlplane-us-west-1 regional cluster)
- 35.198.128.0/22 (controlplane-us-east-1 regional cluster)
- 18.205.32.0/23  (audit and webhook endpoints)

If you prefer FQDN allowlisting we publish these hostnames and support mTLS:
- controlplane.us.redwood-inference.com
- audit.us.redwood-inference.com

Ports/protocols
- TCP/443 (mandatory)
- TCP/853 (optional, DNS-over-TLS)

MAP (mutual action plan)
- 2028-07-18: Redwood (Jonas/Jasmine) — provide draft CIDRs and FQDNs (done).
- 2028-07-19: Aurora — confirm topology and whether static CIDR is acceptable.
- 2028-07-21: Redwood — produce signed evidence pack (SOC snippets + IP digest) and final runbook.

I can join the 07/19 call and we'll prepare a two-page runbook that your firewall team can drop into change control. If you need mTLS certs before the call let us know and we'll pre-provision client cert material for your proxy.

Thanks,
Jasmine Liu
Security Engineer, Redwood Inference

Attachments (for record): egress_arch_options.xlsx, aurora_security_questionnaire_v2.pdf
